identified_problem: D2 rated staged submissions Weak on GenAI exposure and staff workload, and only Moderate on capability verification and authorship assurance. Each unsupervised stage can still be produced by GenAI [R68], [S113], [D03], and practitioners doubted that portfolios resist GenAI on their own [R24]. Marking several drafts adds staff workload [R24], [R04], while AI-permitted take-home marks bunched at the top and agreed only moderately with proctored exam marks [D24], [D25].
recommended_redesign: Keep stages few and tie each to a real milestone (for example design, build and final), with the design stage completed before GenAI is used for low-level code [R82], [R79].
Make at least one checkpoint an individual explanation or short viva on the student's own staged work, so that drafts are not treated as proof of understanding [R79], [S113], [J4].
Weight stage marks towards justification of decisions and critique of AI output against the marking rubric, not towards interim products alone [R23], [R47].
Offset the added marking by reducing assessed tasks elsewhere and by having a tutor team mark stages with one shared rubric [R23], [R47], [R24].
justification: Finding: in a non-computing course of 363 students, a three-phase task with a graded ChatGPT-critique stage ran with tutorial instructors marking, and most students did well on the critique, although a few rated inaccurate AI content highly [R47]. In two engineering cohorts of 14 and 15, three checkpoints with mandatory prompt logs were paired with an individual viva [R79], and in a computing course of about 30 students a guided design phase with screencast code tours gave more meaningful outcome data than the instruments it replaced [R82]. Interpretation: staging makes the process visible and lets AI use be sequenced, but it verifies individual capability only when a stage requires the student to explain or defend their own work under observed conditions [R79], [S113].
implementation_considerations: Cohort size: workable in small cohorts with feedback at each checkpoint and an individual viva [R79]. No staged computing deployment of 50-200 students was reported, and the only large-cohort evidence is a non-computing course of 363 marked by tutorial instructors [R47].

Staff time: budget tutor time for every marking point, and expect open-ended staged projects to lose autograding [R82], [R24]. In team projects, a 5-15 minute one-to-one tutor conversation on artefacts and commit history, at about one tutor per three teams, is a feasible individual check [J4].

Cost and policy: infrastructure needs are low, because staged tasks can be built from existing tasks with modest changes to criteria [R47], [R23]. Hiring freezes and course-approval processes can still delay or limit changes [R24].

Equity: staged written work may suit students who struggle with timed or live formats, but adding in-class questioning raises concerns for neurodivergent and anxious students and students needing accommodations [R04], [R51]. Specify AI tools that all students can access, because unequal access to paid tools was raised [R23], [R01].
Quality assurance: pre-test each stage brief with GenAI before release [R23].
evidence_status_basis: The closest tested redesigns are R47 (computing = N; psychology, n = 363; a three-phase assignment with a graded ChatGPT-critique stage and tracked-changes revision, compared with a 2022 cohort) and R79 (computing = Partial; an ESP32 engineering project in two cohorts of 14 and 15 with three checkpoints, team prompt logs and an individual viva; descriptive statistics only, no comparison group). No study with computing = Y in tested_redesigns.md implemented and evaluated a staged design. R82 reports a staged computing project of about 30 students, but it is a guidance paper with an experience report and is not in the tested index. Validation would need a computing course that compares a staged design with a viva checkpoint against a single-submission design, and records staff marking time.
risks_and_limits: Staging does not stop GenAI producing each unsupervised stage, including plans, reflections and justifications, as the team's Strategy C already notes [R68], [D03]. No study showed that staged drafts or logs are themselves resistant to AI fabrication, and no controlled computing study compared staged with single-submission assessment. No computing study measured marking time for staged work in cohorts over 200, and equity effects have not been evaluated.
